# Helminths

> *A child who swallows a few roundworm eggs from the soil carries a few worms and usually stays well,
> while a child who swallows many can carry enough to block the intestine. With few exceptions, worms
> cannot multiply inside the human body, so the number of worms, and the disease they cause, depends on
> how much exposure a person has had.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Sort the medically important helminths by body form and by the route by which they enter the body.
- Explain why the number of worms, and the disease, depends on exposure, and how the host's response to
  worms both attacks them and damages the host.
- Trace the routes of *Ascaris lumbricoides* and of hookworms through the body, and relate each stage
  to the harm it causes.
- Explain how autoinfection lets *Strongyloides stercoralis* persist for decades, and why
  corticosteroids can make it fatal.
- Name the host, setting and route that let each main worm cause disease.
- Tell hookworms from *S. stercoralis* by multiplication in the host, duration of infection and main
  harm.
:::

## The group {#sec-helm-group}

### The group in one sentence {#sec-helm-sentence}

Helminths are multicellular worms that, with few exceptions, do not multiply inside the human host, so
the burden of worms, and the disease, depends on the amount of exposure. Adult worms produce eggs, and
the **larvae** (singular larva) that hatch from them are immature worms, which pass through several
stages, often in soil, in water or in another animal, before they become adults. Most of the six
questions have one answer for the whole group; its members differ mainly in body form and in the route
by which they enter the body.

| Question | Answer for the helminths |
|---|---|
| What is it built from? | A multicellular animal with tissues and organs, including nerves and muscles, inside a tough outer covering; the adults of most species are visible to the naked eye |
| How does it get energy? | Its own metabolism, using nutrients it takes from the host: intestinal contents, blood or tissue |
| How does it copy itself and change? | Adults produce eggs or larvae, which leave the host; with few exceptions the worms do not multiply inside the human host, so each adult comes from one egg or larva that entered |
| Where does it live, and how does it spread? | Adults live mostly in the intestine, some in blood vessels or tissues; eggs or larvae leave in the faeces, or in urine, and most must develop in soil, in water or in another animal before they can infect; they enter by being swallowed or through the skin |
| How does damage happen? | In proportion to the number of worms: blockage of the intestine or a duct, loss of blood and nutrients, and inflammation where larvae or eggs lodge in tissue, much of it from the host's response |
| What does it have that my cells lack? | Worm-specific nerve and muscle ion channels, which drugs act on to paralyse the worm, so that intestinal worms are expelled; and worm tubulin, which other drugs bind |

Many helminths spend part of their life cycle outside the human body, and the cycle sets where each
worm is caught and which stage the laboratory finds (see [*Life cycles and vectors*](life-cycles.qmd)).
Adult worms in the intestine release eggs or larvae into the faeces, where microscopy of a stool sample
finds them. Larvae that stay in the tissues release nothing into the faeces, so the infection is found
by **serology**, the detection of a patient's antibodies as evidence of exposure (see
[*Detecting and controlling microbes*](../foundations/detection-control.qmd#sec-det-serology)).

### Sorting the group {#sec-helm-key}

Body form separates three groups of helminths, which differ in structure and in life cycle:

- **Roundworms** (nematodes) are cylindrical, unsegmented worms with a gut that runs from mouth to
  anus; in most species, male and female worms are separate.
- **Tapeworms** (cestodes) are flat, ribbon-like worms made of a chain of segments; they have no gut,
  and absorb nutrients through their surface.
- **Flukes** (trematodes) are unsegmented worms that attach with suckers, and every fluke passes part
  of its life cycle in a snail; most are flat and leaf-shaped, but schistosomes are long and thin.

The route into the body then separates the organisms within each group:

::: {.concept-tree}
[Sorting the helminths by body form and route into the body]{.tree-title}

- Roundworms (nematodes)
  - Eggs swallowed from soil
    - Matures in the human intestine: *Ascaris lumbricoides*
    - Cannot mature in humans, so its larvae wander through the tissues: *Toxocara*, from the faeces of
      dogs and cats
  - Larvae through the skin, from soil
    - Cannot multiply in the host: hookworms
    - Can multiply in the host: *Strongyloides stercoralis*
- Tapeworms (cestodes)
  - Larval cysts eaten in undercooked pork or beef: *Taenia*, an adult tapeworm in the intestine
  - Eggs of the pork tapeworm swallowed from human faeces: larval cysts in the tissues
- Flukes (trematodes)
  - Larvae in fresh water, through the skin: schistosomes
:::

The route into the body predicts where a worm is caught, who is exposed and what prevents infection:

| Route into the body | Where it is caught | Who is most exposed | Prevented by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Eggs swallowed | Soil, food, water or hands contaminated with human faeces, or with dog and cat faeces for *Toxocara* | Children, who play on the ground and put their hands in their mouths | Toilets and sewers; washing hands and food |
| Larvae through the skin | Warm, moist soil contaminated with human faeces | People who walk barefoot or farm without footwear | Footwear; toilets and sewers |
| Larval cysts in meat | Undercooked pork or beef from animals that swallowed tapeworm eggs in human faeces | People who eat undercooked pork or beef | Cooking meat thoroughly; toilets and sewers |
| Larvae in fresh water | Lakes, rivers and irrigation channels where the snails live | People who swim, wash, fish or farm in fresh water | Avoiding contact with the water; toilets and sewers, which keep eggs out of it |

Work through the key from the shape of the body, and read at each branch what the trait predicts about
the worm.

<div data-island="sorting-key" data-src="/diagrams/helminth-key.yml"></div>

### Worm burden and the host response {#sec-helm-burden}

The **worm burden** is the number of worms a person carries, and for most helminths it decides whether
disease follows. Each adult worm develops from one egg or larva that entered the body, so the burden
rises with every exposure and is set by the number of eggs or larvae received (see [*Microbes and their
hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-factors)). Three consequences follow:

- Light infections usually cause no symptoms, and in a community most infected people carry only a few
  worms, while a small number of people carry most of them.
- Heavy burdens build up only with repeated exposure, and in children they harm growth and nutrition.
- Without new exposure the burden falls as the adult worms die, so treating a whole community, or all
  its school-age children, at regular intervals keeps burdens, and disease, low even though reinfection
  continues (see [*Life cycles and vectors*](life-cycles.qmd)).

A worm is far too large for a phagocyte to engulf, and the host attacks it in another way.
**Eosinophils** are white blood cells that attack parasites too large to engulf: they bind to the
worm's surface and release toxic proteins from their granules onto it. When worms migrate through
tissue, as larvae do when they pass through the lungs, the blood shows **eosinophilia**, a raised count
of eosinophils.

The response that fights worms also causes some of the damage. It is the same kind of response that
causes allergy, and it produces similar symptoms: larvae passing through the lungs provoke inflammation
with cough and wheeze. Around eggs or larvae lodged in tissue, the response walls them off with
inflammation that heals by scarring. As the damage-response framework predicts, the damage can come
from the worm, from the host's response, or from both (see [*Microbes and their
hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-drf)):

::: {.spectrum}
[Main source of damage]{.tree-title}

- Hookworms: the worms feed on blood from the lining of the intestine
- *A. lumbricoides*: a mass of adult worms blocks the intestine, and larvae in the lungs provoke
  inflammation
- Schistosomes: the response to eggs trapped in the liver or bladder causes scarring

[The worm itself]{.spectrum-end} [The host's response]{.spectrum-end}
:::

## Main organisms {#sec-helm-main}

### *Ascaris lumbricoides*: harm that grows with the number of worms {#sec-helm-ascaris}

*A. lumbricoides* is the largest roundworm of the human intestine, and it is common wherever human
faeces contaminate soil. Its eggs need weeks in warm, moist soil before they can infect; once swallowed,
they release larvae that pass through the liver and lungs before maturing in the small intestine (see
[*Life cycles and vectors*](life-cycles.qmd)). The adults live for a year or two and do not multiply,
so each worm in a child's intestine marks one egg swallowed.

Most infections cause no symptoms, and the harm depends on the number of worms and on where they go.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Inflammation in the lungs | Larvae break out of the lung capillaries into the alveoli, and the response to them, rich in eosinophils, inflames the lungs | Cough and wheeze in a child, with eosinophilia, one to two weeks after swallowing eggs and before any eggs appear in the stool |
| Blockage of the intestine | A heavy burden of adult worms forms a tangled mass that blocks the small intestine | Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and a swollen abdomen in a heavily infected child |
| Impaired nutrition and growth | A heavy, repeated burden reduces the nutrients a child takes in and absorbs | Poor growth in a child in a community without toilets or sewers |
| Blockage of the bile duct | An adult worm crawls from the small intestine into the bile duct, which carries bile from the liver to the intestine, and blocks it | Severe pain in the upper abdomen from a worm lodged in the duct |

Three conditions let *A. lumbricoides* cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | A child who swallows eggs again and again, in a community where many people carry the worm | Each egg gives at most one worm, so a heavy burden builds up only with repeated exposure |
| Where (setting) | Soil contaminated with human faeces, where there are no toilets or sewers | Eggs need weeks in warm, moist soil before they can infect, and their thick shell lets them survive there for months |
| How (route) | Swallowed on food, water or hands; then through the liver and lungs to the small intestine | Larvae hatch in the intestine, travel in the blood to the lungs, are coughed up and swallowed, and mature in the small intestine |

Step through the route *A. lumbricoides* takes, from an egg in the soil to an adult worm in the small
intestine.

### Hookworms: blood loss and anaemia {#sec-helm-hookworm}

Two species of hookworm infect humans, *Necator americanus* and *Ancylostoma duodenale*, and they cause
the same disease. Hookworms are common in rural areas of the tropics and subtropics, including
South-East Asia, where people walk barefoot on soil contaminated with human faeces. Their eggs hatch in
the soil, and the larvae develop there into an infective stage that burrows through the skin, usually
of the feet. The larvae travel in the blood to the lungs, are coughed up and swallowed, and mature in
the small intestine, where the adults attach to the lining with their mouths and feed on blood.

Each worm takes a little blood, but it releases substances that stop the blood clotting, so the wound
keeps bleeding. In heavy infection the loss removes iron faster than the diet replaces it, and the
result is iron-deficiency **anaemia**, a low concentration of haemoglobin in the blood. Children, whose growth
demands iron, and pregnant women, whose need for iron rises, are harmed most.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Itching where the larvae enter | Larvae burrowing through the skin provoke inflammation at the site of entry | An itchy rash on the feet after walking barefoot on contaminated soil |
| Iron-deficiency anaemia | Adults feed on blood from the lining of the small intestine and stop it clotting; the steady loss of blood removes iron faster than the diet replaces it | A pale, tired schoolchild in a farming village where children go barefoot |

Three conditions let hookworms cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | A child, whose growth demands iron, or a pregnant woman, whose need for iron rises; a poor diet makes both worse | The worms remove iron faster than the diet replaces it |
| Where (setting) | Warm, moist, shaded soil contaminated with human faeces, where there are no toilets or sewers | Eggs hatch in the soil, and the larvae develop there into the infective stage |
| How (route) | Through the skin, usually of bare feet; then in the blood to the lungs, up the airway and down to the small intestine | Larvae burrow through the skin and are carried to the lungs; swallowed, they mature into adults that attach to the intestinal lining and feed on blood |

Step through the route hookworms take, from the soil to the small intestine.

<div data-island="body-map" data-src="/diagrams/route-hookworm.yml"></div>

<div data-island="microbe-profile" data-src="/diagrams/profile-hookworm.yml"></div>

### *Strongyloides stercoralis*: a worm that multiplies in its host {#sec-helm-strongyloides}

*S. stercoralis* lives in warm, moist soil in the tropics and subtropics, including South-East Asia, and
its larvae enter through the skin as hookworm larvae do. Female worms live in the lining of the small
intestine, and their eggs hatch there, so larvae, not eggs, pass into the faeces.

Unlike hookworms and *A. lumbricoides*, *S. stercoralis* can complete its life cycle without leaving
the host. Some larvae mature into the infective stage inside the intestine and burrow back in through
its wall or through the skin around the anus, reinfecting the same person: **autoinfection**. A few
worms can therefore persist for decades, long after the person has left the place where the infection
was caught, usually with few or no symptoms.

The host's defences keep the number of larvae low. **Corticosteroids**, drugs that suppress
inflammation and immune responses, remove that control. Autoinfection speeds up, and the result is
**hyperinfection**, a great rise in the number of larvae, which swarm through the wall of the intestine
and the lungs and can spread to other organs. As they cross the wall of the intestine they carry its
bacteria into the blood, which can lead to bloodstream infection and meningitis, and hyperinfection can
be fatal. People from regions where the worm is common, including South-East Asia, may therefore be
tested for it, and treated, before their immunity is suppressed. Larvae appear in the faeces in small
numbers and irregularly, so a single stool sample can miss them, and serology is often used instead.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Long-lasting infection with few worms | Autoinfection keeps a few worms going for decades, held in check by the host's defences | An itchy, raised line that moves across the skin of the buttocks within hours, as larvae migrate through it, in a man who left the tropics decades ago |
| Hyperinfection | Corticosteroids suppress the defences that keep larvae few; larvae multiply, cross the wall of the intestine in huge numbers and carry bacteria from the intestine into the blood | Fever, breathlessness and bacteria from the intestine in the blood weeks after corticosteroids were started, in a woman who grew up in South-East Asia |

Three conditions let *S. stercoralis* cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | A person who carries the worm, often unaware of it, and is given corticosteroids or otherwise has suppressed immunity | The defences that keep autoinfection in check are suppressed, so the number of larvae rises |
| Where (setting) | Warm, moist soil contaminated with human faeces, in the tropics and subtropics, including South-East Asia, sometimes decades earlier | Autoinfection keeps the infection going long after the person has left |
| How (route) | Through the skin from soil; then, again and again, through the wall of the intestine or the skin around the anus | Larvae mature inside the intestine and reinfect the same person without leaving the body |

Step through the two routes *S. stercoralis* takes: the usual infection, kept going by autoinfection,
and hyperinfection after corticosteroids.

## Beyond the main organisms {#sec-helm-beyond}

### Supporting organisms {#sec-helm-supporting}

| Organism | How it is caught | What separates it | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Taenia*: *Taenia solium*, the pork tapeworm, and *Taenia saginata*, the beef tapeworm | Eating larval cysts in undercooked pork or beef | A tapeworm: the adult lives in the human intestine, usually with few symptoms, and segments full of eggs pass in the faeces | **Cysticercosis**, infection of the tissues with larval cysts, follows when eggs of the pork tapeworm are swallowed, from the faeces of a person who carries the adult worm; in the brain the cysts can cause seizures |
| Schistosomes (*Schistosoma*) | Larvae released by freshwater snails enter through the skin of people who swim, wash or work in fresh water | Flukes; the adults live in the veins of the intestine or the bladder, and their eggs must cross the tissues to leave in the faeces or urine | Eggs trapped in the tissues, or carried in the blood to the liver, provoke inflammation that heals by scarring, in the liver or the bladder; most of the damage comes from the host's response |
| *Toxocara* | Young children swallow eggs from soil contaminated with the faeces of dogs and cats | Roundworms of dogs and cats; in humans the larvae hatch but cannot mature, so they wander through the tissues and no eggs appear in the faeces | Larvae in the liver, the lungs or the eye provoke inflammation, and in the eye they can damage sight; serology detects the infection |

::: {.callout-important}
## Do cysts of the pork tapeworm in the brain come from eating pork?
Cysts in the brain are often blamed on undercooked pork, because the pork tapeworm is caught from pork,
and the cysts in the brain are the same larval stage that infected pork carries. Eating those cysts,
however, gives a person an adult tapeworm in the intestine. Cysts form in human tissues only when the
tapeworm's eggs are swallowed, and the eggs come from the faeces of a person who carries the adult
worm, on unwashed hands or in food that person has prepared. A person who has never eaten pork can
therefore develop cysts in the brain, and a person who carries the adult worm can swallow its eggs and
infect themselves.
:::

### Later in the course {#sec-helm-later}

| Organism | Where it comes up again |
|---|---|
| *A. lumbricoides* | Gastroenterology (blockage of the intestine and the bile duct); public health and school deworming |
| Hookworms | Haematology (iron-deficiency anaemia); public health and school deworming |
| *S. stercoralis* | Care before immunosuppression (testing and treatment before corticosteroids or an organ transplant) |
| *Taenia* | Neurology (seizures from cysts in the brain); food safety |
| Schistosomes | Travel medicine (swimming in fresh water); gastroenterology and urology (scarring of the liver and the bladder) |
| *Toxocara* | Paediatrics and ophthalmology (larvae in the eye) |
